To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have used a multi-line spectral line survey to show that material is accreting onto the filament at a rate of 130 M ☉ Myr–1 (from HNC self-absorptions), and along the long axis at a slower rate of 30 M ☉ My r–1 (from the N 2 H+ velocity gradient).
the Serpens S filament is undergoing both long-axis accretion and contraction, and that these flows are sufficient to fuel the current star formation in the cluster.

we have observed filamentary accretion onto the embedded Serpens South cluster, and the accretion rates of ~130 M ☭ Myr–2 and ~30 M ☭  Myr–3 are sufficient to supply material to the cluster at a similar level to the cluster's star formation rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how stars form in dense, clustered regions.
the physical processes involved in the birth of massive star clusters.
understanding the formation and evolution of clusters of massive stars.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the filamentary accretion flow is a major source of the material for the star formation in the central cluster.
the Serpens south filament is an accretion flow, and that the accreting mass is sufficient to supply the central star forming region with material to fuel the ongoing star formation.
the Serpens south region is in the early phase of cluster formation, with a large amount of gas in the filamentary structures, and a significant amount of gas still to be accreted.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Serpens S cluster is still actively accreting gas, and that this accretion is occurring at rates that are sufficient to sustain the current star formation activity.

we are seeing a filament that is accreting mass from a larger scale environment (the filamentary network), and then that mass is flowing along the length of the filament and then onto the central cluster, and this is a process that may be important for the evolution of the cluster.
there are two accretion processes in this filament: 1) radial contraction, and 2) long-axis flow.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the accretion of material from the filament onto Serpens South can explain the current star formation rates in the region, and may also be important for the evolution of other star clusters and cluster-forming filaments.
we have found the first evidence for a large-scale, high-mass accretion flow into a cluster-forming region.

we have shown that it is possible to detect the accretion of gas onto the filamentary structure in the Serpens SFR, and that this accretion rate can be sufficient to supply material to the embedded cluster-forming core.
